As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

**Ethel Barrymore** (born **Ethel Mae Blyth**; August 15, 1879 – June 18, 1959) was an American actress and a member of the [Barrymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrymore_family "Barrymore family")-[Drew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drew_family "Drew family") family of actors.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) Barrymore was a stage, screen and radio actress whose career spanned six decades, and was regarded as "The First Lady of the American Theatre". She received four nominations for the [Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress"), winning for *[None but the Lonely Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/None_but_the_Lonely_Heart_(film) "None but the Lonely Heart (film)")* (1944).

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ethel_Barrymore&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/EthelBarrymore1896.jpg/250px-EthelBarrymore1896.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EthelBarrymore1896.jpg)

Barrymore, 1896

Barrymore was born Ethel Mae Blyth in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), the second child of the actors [Maurice Barrymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Barrymore "Maurice Barrymore") (whose real name was Herbert Blythe) and [Georgiana Drew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgiana_Drew "Georgiana Drew").[[3]](#cite_note-3) She was named for her father's favorite character in [William Makepeace Thackeray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Makepeace_Thackeray "William Makepeace Thackeray")'s *[The Newcomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Newcomes "The Newcomes").*

She was the sister of actors [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Barrymore "John Barrymore") and [Lionel Barrymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Barrymore "Lionel Barrymore"), the aunt of actor [John Drew Barrymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Drew_Barrymore "John Drew Barrymore") and great-aunt of actress [Drew Barrymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drew_Barrymore "Drew Barrymore"). She was a granddaughter of actress and theater manager [Louisa Lane Drew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisa_Lane_Drew "Louisa Lane Drew") and niece of [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") [matinée idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matinée_idol "Matinée idol") [John Drew, Jr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Drew,_Jr. "John Drew, Jr."). and [Vitagraph Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitagraph_Studios "Vitagraph Studios") stage and screen star [Sidney Drew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._and_Mrs._Sidney_Drew "Mr. and Mrs. Sidney Drew"). She spent her childhood in Philadelphia and attended [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") schools there. In 1884, the family moved to [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") for two years. Barrymore's father exhibited a play and starred on stage plays at [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London")'s [Haymarket Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haymarket_Theatre "Haymarket Theatre").[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4) Returning to the U.S. in 1886, her father took her to her first [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") game, which established her lifelong love of baseball.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ethel_Barrymore&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Ethel_Barrymore%2C_three-quarter_length_portrait%2C_seated%2C_facing_front.jpg/250px-Ethel_Barrymore%2C_three-quarter_length_portrait%2C_seated%2C_facing_front.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ethel_Barrymore,_three-quarter_length_portrait,_seated,_facing_front.jpg)

Barrymore in 1901 in one of the costumes from *Captain Jinks of the Horse Marines*

In the summer of 1893, Barrymore was in the company of her mother Georgie, who had been ailing from [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis") and took a curative [sabbatical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabbatical "Sabbatical") to [Santa Barbara, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Barbara,_California "Santa Barbara, California"), not far from where [family friend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_friend "Family friend") [Helena Modjeska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Modjeska "Helena Modjeska") had a retreat. Georgie did not recover and died in July 1893 at age 36. Essentially Ethel's and Lionel's childhood ended when Georgie died; they were forced to go to work in their teens with neither finishing high school. John, a few years younger, stayed with their grandmother and other relatives. Barrymore's first appearance on Broadway was in 1895, in a play called *[The Imprudent Young Couple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Imprudent_Young_Couple "The Imprudent Young Couple")* which starred her uncle [John Drew Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Drew_Jr. "John Drew Jr.") and [Maude Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maude_Adams "Maude Adams"). She appeared with Drew and Adams again in 1896 in *[Rosemary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosemary_(play) "Rosemary (play)")*.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In 1897 Ethel went with [William Gillette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gillette "William Gillette") to London to play Miss Kittridge in Gillette's *Secret Service*. She was about to return to the States with Gillette's troupe when [Henry Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Irving "Henry Irving") and [Ellen Terry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Terry "Ellen Terry") offered her the role of Annette in *The Bells*. A full London tour was on and, before it was over, Ethel created, on [New Year's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Day "New Year's Day") 1898, Euphrosine in *Peter the Great* at the [Lyceum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyceum_Theatre,_London "Lyceum Theatre, London"), the play having been written by Irving's son, Laurence. Men everywhere were smitten with Ethel, most notably [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill"), who asked her to marry him. Not wishing to be a politician's wife, she refused. Winston, years later, married [Clementine Hozier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clementine_Hozier "Clementine Hozier"), who looked very much like Ethel. Winston and Ethel remained friends until the end of her life.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d9/EthelBarrymoreCarrots.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EthelBarrymoreCarrots.jpg)

Barrymore playing the male character *Carrots* in a [play of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poil_de_carotte "Poil de carotte"), 1902

After her season in London, Ethel returned to the U.S. [Charles Frohman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Frohman "Charles Frohman") cast her first in *Catherine* and then as Stella de Grex in *His Excellency the Governor*.[[7]](#cite_note-7) After that, Frohman finally gave Ethel the role that would make her a star: Madame Trentoni in *Captain Jinks of the Horse Marines*,[[8]](#cite_note-8) which opened at the [Garrick Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrick_Theatre "Garrick Theatre") in London's [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_theatre "West End theatre") on February 4, 1901. Unbeknownst to Ethel, her father Maurice had witnessed the performance as an audience member and walked up to his daughter, congratulated her and gave her a big hug. It was the first and only time he saw her on stage professionally. When the tour concluded in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") in June, she had out-drawn two of the most prominent actresses of her day, [Mrs. Patrick Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrs._Patrick_Campbell "Mrs. Patrick Campbell") and [Minnie Maddern Fiske](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnie_Maddern_Fiske "Minnie Maddern Fiske").

Following her triumph in *Captain Jinks*, Ethel gave sterling performances in many top-rate productions and it was in Thomas Raceward's *Sunday* that she uttered what would be her most famous line, "[That's all there is, there isn't any more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's_all_there_is,_there_isn't_any_more "That's all there is, there isn't any more")."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

She portrayed [Nora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nora_Helmer "Nora Helmer") in *[A Doll's House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Doll's_House "A Doll's House")* by [Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Ibsen "Henrik Ibsen") (1905), and [Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juliet "Juliet") in *[Romeo and Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romeo_and_Juliet "Romeo and Juliet")* by [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") (1922).

**Anna Maria Magnani** (Italian: [[ˈanna maɲˈɲaːni]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian"); 7 March 1908 – 26 September 1973) was an Italian actress.[[1]](#cite_note-WVobit-1) She was the first Italian woman to win an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards").

Born and raised in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), Italy or [Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria "Alexandria"), she worked her way through Rome's Academy of Dramatic Art by singing at night clubs.[[2]](#cite_note-Johnson-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Actors-3) During her career, her only child was stricken by [polio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polio "Polio") when he was 18 months old and remained disabled. She was referred to as "La Lupa", the "perennial toast of Rome" and a "living she-wolf symbol" of the cinema. *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")* described her personality as "fiery", and drama critic [Harold Clurman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Clurman "Harold Clurman") said her acting was "volcanic". In the realm of Italian cinema, she was "passionate, fearless, and exciting", an actress whom film historian Barry Monush calls "the volcanic earth mother of all Italian cinema."[[4]](#cite_note-Monush-4) Director [Roberto Rossellini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Rossellini "Roberto Rossellini") called her "the greatest acting genius since [Eleonora Duse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleonora_Duse "Eleonora Duse")".[[2]](#cite_note-Johnson-2) Playwright [Tennessee Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams") became an admirer of her acting and wrote *[The Rose Tattoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rose_Tattoo_(film) "The Rose Tattoo (film)")* (1955) specifically for her to star in, a role for which she received an [Academy Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress "Academy Award for Best Actress").

After meeting director [Goffredo Alessandrini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goffredo_Alessandrini "Goffredo Alessandrini"), she received her first screen role in *[The Blind Woman of Sorrento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blind_Woman_of_Sorrento_(1934_film) "The Blind Woman of Sorrento (1934 film)")* (*La cieca di Sorrento*, 1934) and later achieved international attention in Rossellini's *[Rome, Open City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome,_Open_City "Rome, Open City")* (1945), which is seen as launching the [Italian neorealism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_neorealism "Italian neorealism") movement in cinema.[[4]](#cite_note-Monush-4) As an actress, she became recognized for her dynamic and forceful portrayals of "earthy lower-class women"[[5]](#cite_note-5) in such films as *[L'Amore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Amore_(film) "L'Amore (film)")* (1948), *[Bellissima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellissima_(film) "Bellissima (film)")* (1951), *The Rose Tattoo* (1955), *[The Fugitive Kind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fugitive_Kind "The Fugitive Kind")* (1960) and *[Mamma Roma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamma_Roma "Mamma Roma")* (1962). As early as 1950, *[Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_(magazine) "Life (magazine)")* had already stated that Magnani was "one of the most impressive actresses since [Garbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo "Greta Garbo")".[[6]](#cite_note-Life50-6)

## Early years

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anna_Magnani&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early years")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/e3/AnnChristie39stage.jpg/250px-AnnChristie39stage.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AnnChristie39stage.jpg)

Acting on stage as *Anna Christie* with [Mario Besesti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Besesti "Mario Besesti"), 1939[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Magnani's parentage and birthplace are uncertain. Some sources suggest she was born in Rome, others suggest Egypt.[[3]](#cite_note-Actors-3) Her mother was Marina Magnani.[[2]](#cite_note-Johnson-2) Film director [Franco Zeffirelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco_Zeffirelli "Franco Zeffirelli"), who claimed to know Magnani well, states in his autobiography that she was born in Alexandria, Egypt, to an Italian-Jewish mother and Egyptian father, and that "only later did she become Roman when her grandmother brought her over and raised her in one of the Roman slum districts."[[8]](#cite_note-Zeffirelli-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) Magnani herself stated that her mother was married in Egypt, but returned to Rome before giving birth to her at [Porta Pia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porta_Pia "Porta Pia"), and did not know how the rumor of her Egyptian birth got started.[[10]](#cite_note-10) She was enrolled in a French convent school in Rome, where she learned to speak French and play the piano. She also developed a passion for acting from watching the nuns stage their Christmas plays. This period of formal education lasted until the age of 14.[[6]](#cite_note-Life50-6)

She was a "plain, frail child with a forlornness of spirit". Her grandparents compensated by pampering her with food and clothes. Yet while growing up, she is said to have felt more at ease around "more earthly" companions, often befriending the "toughest kid on the block".[[6]](#cite_note-Life50-6) This trait carried over into her adult life when she proclaimed, "I hate respectability. Give me the life of the streets, of common people."[[6]](#cite_note-Life50-6)

At age 17, she went on to study at the [Eleonora Duse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleonora_Duse "Eleonora Duse") Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in Rome for two years.[[6]](#cite_note-Life50-6) To support herself, Magnani sang in [nightclubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightclub "Nightclub") and [cabarets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabaret "Cabaret"); leading to her being dubbed "the Italian [Édith Piaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Édith_Piaf "Édith Piaf")". However, her actor friend Micky Knox writes that she "never studied acting formally" and started her career in Italian music halls singing traditional Roman folk songs. "She was instinctive" he writes. "She had the ability to call up emotions at will, to move an audience, to convince them that life on the stage was as real and natural as life in their own kitchen."[[11]](#cite_note-11) Film critic [David Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Thomson_(film_critic) "David Thomson (film critic)") wrote that Magnani was considered an "outstanding theatre actress" in productions of *[Anna Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Christie "Anna Christie")* and *[The Petrified Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Petrified_Forest "The Petrified Forest")*.[[12]](#cite_note-Thomson-12)

## Early acting career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anna_Magnani&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early acting career")]

In 1933, Magnani was acting in experimental plays in Rome when she was discovered by Italian filmmaker [Goffredo Alessandrini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goffredo_Alessandrini "Goffredo Alessandrini").[[6]](#cite_note-Life50-6) The couple married the same year. [Nunzio Malasomma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nunzio_Malasomma "Nunzio Malasomma") directed her in her first major film role in *[The Blind Woman of Sorrento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blind_Woman_of_Sorrento_(1934_film) "The Blind Woman of Sorrento (1934 film)")* (*La Cieca di Sorrento*, 1934). Goffredo Alessandrini directed her in *[Cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry_(1936_Italian_film) "Cavalry (1936 Italian film)")* (*Cavalleria*, 1936). For director [Vittorio De Sica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vittorio_De_Sica "Vittorio De Sica"), Magnani starred in *[Teresa Venerdì](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Venerdì "Teresa Venerdì")* (1941). De Sica called this Magnani's "first true film". In it, she plays Loletta Prima, the girlfriend of De Sica's character, Pietro Vignali. De Sica described Magnani's laugh as "loud, overwhelming, and tragic".[[13]](#cite_note-13)

## Italian stardom

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anna_Magnani&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Italian stardom")]

Magnani became a major star in post-War Italian cinema, coming to international prominence in the films of [Roberto Rossellini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Rossellini "Roberto Rossellini") and other Italian directors.

The **Academy Juvenile Award**, also known informally as the **Juvenile Oscar**, was a [Special Honorary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award") [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") bestowed at the discretion of the [Board of Governors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences#Current_administration_of_the_Academy "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") of the [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") (AMPAS) to specifically recognize [juvenile](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/juvenile "wikt:juvenile") performers under the age of eighteen for their "outstanding contribution[s] to screen entertainment".[[1]](#cite_note-Oscars_22-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_1-2)

The honor was first awarded by the academy at the [7th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_Academy_Awards "7th Academy Awards") to 6-year-old [Shirley Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Temple "Shirley Temple") for her work in [motion pictures of 1934](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1934_in_film "1934 in film").[[2]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_1-2) The Award continued to be presented intermittently over the next 26 years to a total of 12 child actors and actresses, with the last Juvenile Oscar presented at the [33rd Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Academy_Awards "33rd Academy Awards") to 14-year-old [Hayley Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayley_Mills "Hayley Mills") who received the child-size statuette for her performance in the [1960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_in_film "1960 in film") film *[Pollyanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollyanna_(1960_film) "Pollyanna (1960 film)")*.[[3]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_10-3)

The trophy itself was a miniature Academy Award statuette standing an estimated seven inches tall (depending upon variations to its base over time),[[2]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_1-2)[[4]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_4-4)[[5]](#cite_note-TV_Guide-5)[[6]](#cite_note-Variety2-6)[[7]](#cite_note-Variety3-7) approximately half the height of the standard 13.5 inch tall Oscar trophy.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

## Honorary Academy Awards

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Academy_Juvenile_Award&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Honorary Academy Awards")]

Main article: [Academy Honorary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award")

In addition to its competitive [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") of Merit, the [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") (AMPAS) also presents ["Special"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award") or ["Honorary"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award") Academy Awards. These awards are given (typically, annually) by the [Board of Governors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences#Current_administration_of_the_Academy "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") of AMPAS to celebrate motion picture achievements that are not covered by other existing [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") categories.[[9]](#cite_note-HonoraryAbout-9)[[10]](#cite_note-AboutHonoraryAward-10) This includes the awards that had been presented to juvenile actors from 1934 to 1960 (known only informally as the "Juvenile Academy Awards").

Beginning with the [1st Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards") – celebrating film achievements of [1927](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1927_in_film "1927 in film") and [1928](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1928_in_film "1928 in film") – these awards were formally referred to as "Special Awards". The first of these Special Awards was presented to [Charles Chaplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Chaplin "Charlie Chaplin") (for *[The Circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Circus_(1928_film) "The Circus (1928 film)")*) and to [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.") (for *[The Jazz Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Singer "The Jazz Singer")*). Beginning with the [23rd Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd_Academy_Awards "23rd Academy Awards") – celebrating film achievements of [1950](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_in_film "1950 in film") – these Special Awards were formally renamed by the academy as "Honorary Awards". These Honorary Awards continue to be presented today, although the "Juvenile Academy Award" proper has itself been discontinued.

## History of the Academy Juvenile Award

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Academy_Juvenile_Award&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History of the Academy Juvenile Award")]

The Academy Awards, [first presented on May 16, 1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards"), did not initially present a [Special Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award") for juvenile actors.[[11]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_11-11) The very first [child actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_actor "Child actor") to be nominated for an Oscar was 9-year-old [Jackie Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Cooper "Jackie Cooper"), who was nominated as [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") in 1931 for his work in the film *[Skippy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skippy_(1931_film) "Skippy (1931 film)")*. Cooper, however, lost that year to [Lionel Barrymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Barrymore "Lionel Barrymore").[[12]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_12-12) Recognizing that children could be placed at a disadvantage in the hearts and minds of Academy voters when nominated alongside their adult counterparts in the competitive [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") and [Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress "Academy Award for Best Actress") categories[[13]](#cite_note-Reuters-13) – and with no categories for [Best Supporting Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor") or [Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress") having yet been created[[14]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_13-14) – the academy saw the need to establish an Honorary "Special Award" specifically to recognize juveniles under the age of eighteen for their work in film.[[2]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_1-2)

On February 27, 1935, the [7th Annual Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_Academy_Awards "7th Academy Awards"), honoring achievements in film for the year 1934, became the first Oscar ceremony at which the Special Juvenile Award was presented.[[2]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_1-2) Playfully dubbed the "Oscarette" by [Bob Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hope "Bob Hope") in 1945,[[15]](#cite_note-Hollywoodland_1-15) the statuette itself was a miniaturized Oscar, depicting an [Art Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Deco "Art Deco") image of a [knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight "Knight") holding a [crusader's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades "Crusades") [sword](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword "Sword") and standing on a [reel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reel "Reel") of film.[[16]](#cite_note-Gold_Encyclopedia-16) Standing approximately one-half the size of its full-sized counterpart, this rare child-sized trophy remained the [prototype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prototype "Prototype") for the statuette throughout the history of the Award, with only relatively small modifications to its base over time.[[5]](#cite_note-TV_Guide-5)[[17]](#cite_note-Los_Angeles_Times_2-17)[[18]](#cite_note-Variety-18)

After first being presented in 1935, the Special Juvenile Award continued to be presented intermittently to a total of 12 young actors and actresses over the next 26 years.[[5]](#cite_note-TV_Guide-5)[[19]](#cite_note-Mental_Floss-19) However, there were several juvenile actors who were instead nominated in the competitive Best Supporting Actor/Actress categories during this time. These included, most notably: 14-year-old [Bonita Granville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonita_Granville "Bonita Granville") as Best Supporting Actress of 1936 for *[These Three](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/These_Three "These Three")*;[[20]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_14-20) 11-year-old [Brandon deWilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_deWilde "Brandon deWilde") as Best Supporting Actor of 1953 for *[Shane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_(film) "Shane (film)")*;[[21]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_15-21) 17-year-old [Sal Mineo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sal_Mineo "Sal Mineo") as Best Supporting Actor of 1955 for *[Rebel Without a Cause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebel_Without_a_Cause "Rebel Without a Cause")*;[[22]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_16-22) and 11-year-old [Patty McCormack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patty_McCormack "Patty McCormack") as Best Supporting Actress of 1956 for *[The Bad Seed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bad_Seed_(1956_film) "The Bad Seed (1956 film)")*.[[23]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_17-23) All of these nominees, however, lost to their adult counterparts in their respective categories.

Held on April 17, 1961, the [33rd Annual Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Academy_Awards "33rd Academy Awards"), honoring achievements in film for the year 1960, was the last Oscar ceremony at which the Honorary Juvenile Award was presented.[[3]](#cite_note-Oscars.org_10-3)

### Upsystem: [Mercury](/world/mercury), Downsystem: [The Moon](/world/moon)

#### [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus) is the closest planet in the solar system to Earth's size and gravity - but the atmosphere is much heavier and hotter. The pressure on the surface is the equivalent of being 1km underwater on Earth - and the temperature is hot enough to melt lead. So visiting features on the surface would be challenging. However, 50 km above the ground the pressure and temperature [are quite nice](http://motherboard.vice.com/read/why-we-should-build-cloud-cities-on-venus).
